VideoTitle: Affirmative Action is Racist (Part 2) | Change My Mind
CommentText: You asked so here is my comment on affirmative action. Disclosure, I am a 65, soon to be 66-year-old polio survivor. I began walking around 4 years old and have no use of my left arm. I was blessed to be able to get around and function in life. I still function but require an electric scooter to get around with a power seat lift in order to stand up. I also did get a handicap license plate as I hit my fifties because of a true need in order to avoid long distances as my legs began weakening further. When I was 19 years old back in 1975, I had completed a technical Programming degree at Control Data Institute. I applied at several places and had a very positive interview with a hospital records processing center in DeKalb County outside of Atlanta. The manager I interviewed with basically told me I had the position but he had to okay it with the Hospital. I followed up with my interviewer via phone, everything was good and I was excited about the opportunity. I followed up again and the tone had changed. He was very apologetic but the Hospital had told him that they needed to hire a black person and a black lady I went to school with fit the requirement along with checking another box, being female. I ended up finding a job as a Computer Operator at a Bank in Atlanta which delayed my entry into the Programming field for 3.5 years. I wasn't happy, however I refused to use my disabilities as a way to obtain the position because I felt it was wrong. I've never used it for advantage over another person. I believe that after my experience over 46 years ago, it is time to end affirmative action, enough Americans have been discriminated against and suffered for what they had nothing to do with using this racially discriminatory law. It is no more justifiable than if I had used my disability to wrest the Programming position from my former classmate or anyone. It would have made me no better than those who take positions from others based on race as opposed to merit. These types of advantages imposed against others are also an anchor around the neck of America as a whole. I watched our nation excel to the Moon and leave other nations in the dust. Not so much any longer. We no longer emphasize the best making it to important top positions. We allow race, sex and sexual orientation to trump superior intellect and abilities.

def fibDPTabulation(position):
    if position <= 1: return 1
    table = list()
    table = [0 for i in range(0, position+1)]
    table[1] = 1
    
    length = len(table)
    for i in range(2, length):
        table[i] = table[i-2] + table[i-1]
    
    return table[position]

VideoTitle: Inside the brain of a gambling addict - BBC News
CommentText:
I've been in the online slots world for about a year now, I've never considered myself an addict, and if I go by raw numbers, I could say that I've probably won 90% of what I've lost, (let's say I've lost $1000 and won $900, maybe I've even won more than I lost, I'm not keeping count) what I'm noticing is that if you don't control your impulses this can become very dangerous. Anyway, when I win, or have won, I've always withdrawn 80% of that capital to use it, and I've bought useful things with that money won, however, there's always that "what if maybe..." and you end up going back, because you think you'll win again, and I suspect that online casinos are tracking players so that when they detect that they've won, they'll start draining all the money possible to recover the loss. And even today it is more dangerous, because they can do it perfectly with the information from the internet and with a simple follow-up of your activity in their online casinos. I have not fallen into addiction, luckily, but I have relatives who have, and it is very sad. I plan not to gamble again, but sometimes I go back just for fun, I have never used all my capital or my monthly earnings, but I have used small amounts that added up to important parts of my capital.

I will give some advice: always look at your percentages used, not just the numbers, percentage of your capital that has resulted in profits, or losses. And another thing, if you win, withdraw immediately, especially if it is an online casino. Anyway, as many people say; the best way to win is not to play, remember that casinos are literally traps, otherwise, they would not exist. But if you do not see yourself capable of quitting, start reducing your risks, use the money on what you later regretted not using, when you can use it. Give gifts to your loved ones, or learn to invest in stocks and in the market. And set a loss limit, never break it (I know you will) but try as hard as possible not to do so, be loyal to yourself. This will avoid many problems and regrets.

In the first iteration,

VideoTitle: Why React.js is taking a new direction
CommentText:
One question I rarely see addressed in these discussions of moving computation back to the server - isn't that expensive? If your app scales to a million users, or even more, and most of the work is done client side, there's no/little extra cost to host it.

But now using a framework like remix, even with caching, there's going to be more and more computation on the server as you get more users and that costs more. As you mention in the video that's not a problem for big companies like Facebook but the whole point of these improvements is to make this easier for small teams, right? A surprise $100k AWS fee because your app went viral, or getting cut off by Vercel at exactly the point where you're getting popular is a problem. Doing most of the work client side prevents this problem.

Until I see this issue clearly and directly addressed I'm going to stick with the old way. I've chosen not to use Remix for this reason.

To add about self-hosting. I've played around with self-hosting for a long time. I literally just jumped into it with absolutely no idea what I was doing which I honestly think is the best way to learn. Domain names are paid yearly, I highly recommend a legitimate one like Namecheap. Many of the others like GoDaddy are legitimate and legal but very shady and sneaky. You can get one for like $3 or $5 for the entire year, just that one $5 flat fee. You don't need anything expensive.


For a server the best bet is just a completely blank remote computer. Digital Ocean provides this, their not-shady, their completely legitimate, and their cheapest computer is $5 a month. They have a wonderful pricing model with no hidden costs, fees, etc... that many companies hide away in fine print. The downside is your going to start working with nothing, you have a blank Linux computer with nothing on it, not even a webserver. So, yes, you'll have to set that up yourself. I'd even sugest getting a friend to help you if you don't want to jump in. But It's $5 a month, with a great company, great pricing model, and you have total control of the server so it's worth it.


Anyways, if your interested in the self-hosting option ~_^

CommentText:
A common problem in user interface involves imposing a stable order upon elements displayed upon a page. While the initial order is easy to specify, keeping it consistent with user actions is interesting.

Take for example a menu structure that looks something like this :

Apple
  Sour
  Green
  Red
Banana
  Ripe
  Raw
  Fried
    Spicy
    Sweet
    Salted
Cats
  Large
    Black
    White
  Small
    Grey
    Striped
                            
Now imagine an operation on this structure that drag-drops an element from any position to any position in the tree.

For example, moveBelow(Apple/Red, Banana/Fried/Spicy).

The (strange) new tree after this operation looks as shown below. The Red element is now sitting under Banana/Fried/Spicy as specified.

Apple
  Sour
  Green
Banana
  Ripe
  Raw
  Fried
    Spicy
    Red
    Sweet
    Salted
Cats
  Large
    Black
    White
  Small
    Grey
    Striped
                            
Note that it is possible to move not just leaf elements but also subtree, as in moveBelow (Banana/Fried, Cats/Small). This yields an even stranger tree as shown below. The entire Fried submenu is now placed after Cats/Small, on the path Cats/Fried.

Apple
  Sour
  Green
Banana
  Ripe
  Raw
Cats
  Large
    Black
    White
  Small
    Grey
    Striped
  Fried
    Spicy
    Red
    Sweet
    Salted

                              
Implement a data structure to represent the menu, and the function moveBelow (fromPath, belowPath)

Use any programming language you like. The function should operate upon the data structure and leave it in a correct state after it is done; it should be possible to see the order (and path!) of each element in the datastructure.

Make sure photos and documents are on a hard drive and in a box with other important items, let's call this a fire box. 
Make sure you have a fire plan for your neighbourhood, house and region. 
Make sure your property is cleaned at least once a year or once a month depending where you are. 
Put a sign on the outside about what pets you have inside, this will be great for any type of emergency in your house and people will know who's inside, pets or elderly or disabled even. 
Make sure you listen to everything the fire department tells you.

25:40 so here's the explanation and my understanding of this particular example ---
The onclick here requires a reference of a function so that it can call it when the click event occurs on corresponding button, we always pass reference in this type of situation to prevent the function to get executed immediately. 
But the problem is we can't just pass the reference of the function because as we know it requires the color in the form of parameter and we are noy storing the reference in variable like structure such as let refHolder = clickHandler; so we can't call the refHolder later with the color parameter later in code such as refHolder('blue'). 
In reality, we are giving the reference to onclick which doesn't have an in built functionality or human intelligence to call this clickHandler with argument based on the button. 
So now we actually have a tiny war between onclick() demanding a reference and clickHandler(color) which demands to be called with a parameter only otherwise error. 

Now in order to fullfill the demand of bith entities, we can we will indeed call the clickHandler() with color parameter passed ( demand fulfilled ) but at the same time we will do something that a reference is given to onClick function ( which it strictly demands ), we will return reference of an inner function which does the main work or logic( demand fulfilled ) ( Very important thing to note here is this could not have been achieved without the feature of lexical scoping )

VideoTitle: How I Failed the Google Coding Interview (and lessons I learned)
CommentText: Having conducted numerous coding question interviews, I'd like to offer some insights from the interviewer's perspective. It seems you likely struggled in the first two coding rounds. Also, in my experience, a rejection notice wouldn't take three weeks unless you were a strong contender. Two general points: The biggest issue arises when an over-prepared applicant (the "competitive coder" type) receives a straightforward question they recognize and immediately dives in without much communication. Whether they go down the wrong path or not is secondary. What matters most is seeing how a candidate tackles an unfamiliar problem; it's not just about reaching the solution. Remember: The interviewer already knows the answer; they're interested in your approach. Bonus: If you recognize an interview question (from practice, etc.), tell the interviewer immediately. Solving it instantly wastes their time, forcing them to ask another question with less time. Pretending you don't know it won't work; programmers are bad actors, and they'll be even more frustrated. Most interviewers have backup questions prepared. As for the nodding and letting you make mistakes, that's normal for a good interviewer. Interviewing is like walking a dog; you let them explore a bit, reeling them in when needed, but not holding them too tightly. Often, candidates explain their intended solution, and you know it's wrong, but you let them proceed (unless they've misunderstood the problem) to see what happens. Interviewers find this hard because they must suppress their helpful instincts, which they use daily at work. Nods, smiles, and remarks like "mmh, interesting" or "okay" aren't positive or negative signals; they're just polite gestures. Don't get overconfident; realize you're on your own at that moment. The same applies to general conversation; the interviewer might ask probing questions but generally won't add anything new, only helping you think or bounce ideas, like playing tennis with a wall. It's mostly about letting you succeed or fail independently. Remember: The interviewer isn't trying to help; they're trying NOT to help. Corollary: If the interviewer gives a helpful tip, you're likely behind schedule. A good interviewer will subtly insert the tip during conversation. But if they interrupt you entirely to give an obvious tip, you're far off track and struggling with communication, as it's probably not their first attempt to guide you.

VideoTitle: How I Failed the Google Coding Interview (and lessons I learned)
CommentText: The thing I find problematic about this video is that while it's meant to be about a failed coding interview, it never actually details how you failed. The summary is basically, 'I didn't have the right answer right away.' This message can increase stress when taking these interviews. Simply stating 'think harder' doesn't offer useful guidance for preparation. As you mentioned initially, knowing how the failures contributed to future success would be helpful. For instance, did you increase your focus on algorithms? Did you refine your list of algorithms to memorize? Or did you concentrate more on big-O efficiency? The extra detail like 'Google just wants reasonable people' wasn't very helpful, given that you were presumably already reasonable in the first interview. On a positive note, you did mention that misinterpreting code is a critical error to avoid, which is an absolutely important point and it is very likely that coding interviewers will be specifically looking out for these kinds of misinterpretations of the problem.

VideoTitle: Git and GitHub for Beginners - Crash Course
CommentText: I feel relieved, I'm finally grasping this! Thank you for this tutorial, and thank you Gwen for taking the time to create it! Edit: After watching the tutorial again, I have a couple of suggestions: 1. When making tutorials, you need to really understand the importance of adjusting your pace to that of the learner. You start with a great overview of key terms, then quickly introduce both advanced and beginner ideas together, which just confuses the viewer. Slow down, explain things simply, that's what we need. 2. On the topic of mixing concepts, it's fine to keep tutorials short and add footnotes for the advanced stuff. This allows the beginner to focus on the basics, and they can access the footnotes when they're ready, making that content more effective. After all, isn't being efficient key to programming? I used to hate being forced to take English classes as a CS student, but now I see why. I spent 4 hours debugging a Terminal issue, just to learn that it was because the tutorial told the user to paste the following command into the terminal: *eval "$(ssh-agent exec -s)"* Meaning, including the quotation marks. After 4 hours of research into chmod, File Links, Groups, root directories, Inodes, things I knew nothing about, I fixed the problem by removing the quotation marks. A know-it-all dev might say, 'That's obvious', but no! The instructions said 'paste', which means: - Select code - ctrl+c on Windows (cmd+c on Mac) - ctrl+v/cmd+v in Terminal. Either the tutorial should've been: *eval $(ssh-agent exec -s)* , or the writer should have clarified the removal of quotes. As software development becomes more collaborative, engineers can't get away with being asocial or bad communicators, so this is something that many need to improve on.

VideoTitle: How Falling Behind Can Get You Ahead | David Epstein | TEDxManchester
CommentText:
When I was younger, I went through a boot camp course to teach us on the mindset of being a successful person. I remembered clearly, on the first day, when the host asked us why are we here. Some kid just replied that they are here because they want to ace their academic examinations. The host simply knocked his head on the whiteboard for a few times, contemplating on how to translate the message. 

It took me a few decades to finally understand that, it's not getting education scoring and being a money-making machine that will get you far. Sure, money is an essential basic to survival in this economy, but it's not everything, even if you make the most money in this world, it is pointless if you have no idea what you are doing in your life. 

Successful people don't go for top scores in their academic results nor do they go for the money. Even if they do, that's because they know what they want. It's just a pawn in their chess, and it's not everything. The whole point is simple; They just do what they love and they just keep on doing that. This is true success, so what even if you enjoy doing the most redundant and the most insignificant things in life unlike your neighbor who is getting married and moving out being a top-notch lawyer or something else while you are still hiding in you mum's basement.. Take your time, quality over quantity, be yourself, stop comparing and don't follow everybody else' footstep.

That's the whole lesson that took me decades to learn while fortunate people in this era can learn within a 14min video.

VideoTitle: 06 Virtual DOM, Fibre and reconciliation
CommentText:
Thank you so much Hitesh sir
Here is the takeaway from the video
/* 
1.The createRoot create's its own DOM and then compare it with the web browser's DOM and only update those components which are actually updated.
2.But the browser removes the whole DOM and then recrates the whole DOM with the updated values this is called reload.
3. However virtual DOM tracks whole DOM like a tree like structure and updates only those values which were only changed.
4. But some values depends on network call so if we update a value it might get update immediately via a network call.
5. So we will have to update it again. To avoid this overhead we can drop the updation calls for the immediate value update.
6. The current algo used by the React is called the React Fibre algo.
7. The algo react uses to differentiate the web browser's tree and React's tree formed through create root is called reconciliation.
8. Reconciliation is the algo behind what popularly known as the Virtual-DOM.
9.In UI it is not necessary for every update to be applied immediately. */

React Native vs Flutter
CommentText:
I have used all 4 to build apps, and I personally prefer Flutter. The closer you get to native the better, and dart is really easy to learn and use. It still has a way to go to before it's as fleshed out as some of the other options (looking at you maps), but otherwise I have been able to create some really complex apps with it. Also if you are coming from RN background, then you will be happy to know that you can use Redux with it.

I will however say that RN is a better choice if you will be using "standard" widgets instead of custom designed ones when time is of importance. Since RN adaptively displays the widgets for each platform. Speeding up your development time and making your app appear native for both iOS and Android users respectively, without any extra effort from your end.

VideoTitle: Design Youtube - System Design Interview
CommentText:
Nosql used for metadata since uploads are frequent mandating sharding. But I don't think Mongodb is suitable to Youtube since it isn't good for Availability. There is a downtime when the master is down to elect the next master from slaves. I would prefer Cassandra due to its high availability (leaderless). But Cassandra isn't good when there are read queries on multiple attributes. Hence I would couple Cassandra with Elasticsearch inturn bringing in Fuzzysearch.
If it were Netflix, I would have sticked onto a simple Mysql since writes are not frequent and provides enough querying. If fuzzy search required, I would still couple it with ES. (Would never use an ES as a primary db since unreliable).

VideoTitle: What animals are thinking and feeling, and why it should matter | Carl Safina | TEDxMidAtlantic
CommentText: We live in northwestern Minnesota.  We have not always lived here.  Deer hunting season is a big event.  The town's newspaper includes photos of young kids posed with the head of the dead deer they just shot.  When you drive from little town to little town, deer stands jut out all year in low lying areas.  If you care about deer, you are the odd man out.  We don't hunt at our house.  Rather, we enjoy seeing the deer visit our property.   There  have been more than a few times when I bonded with a particular deer.  A few years ago, I noticed a doe that liked to frequent our yard.  One day, she laid down very near our patio door and gave birth to her two fawns right in that spot.  Did she trust us?  Obviously.  The summer and fall months went by, and the three of them (as well as others) frequented our yard on an almost daily basis.  The fawns grew and lost their spots.  Deer hunting season was around the corner and with dread, I counted down the days.  On the first day of deer hunting season, I saw her run past our house at high speed with her fawns behind.  I never saw her again.  Deer season went on.  We'd hear gunshots whenever we were outside.  Getting the mail.  Gunshots.  Taking the dog out to potty.  Gunshots.  Several weeks of deer hunting season.  No deer frequented our yard as the weeks went on.  Finally, the season ended.  It was the day after.  It was a grey, dull November day.  I looked out our living room window and saw an older fawn (her fawn?) stand in the woods on the border of what was "our yard".  It had its ears back, its coat was scuffled up, and it stood there and stared at the house ... and at me.  I figured it was one of the fawns and probably the only one left of her family.  I never saw it again.

VideoTitle: Climbing Stairs - Dynamic Programming - Leetcode 70 - Python
CommentText:
def climbStairs(self, n: int) -> int:
        penultimate, ultimate = 0, 1
        for i in range(n):
            penultimate, ultimate = ultimate, penultimate + ultimate
        return ultimate

This also works as a solution.
1. We take n steps via range(n)
2. We don't need a temp var, since we shift over the penultimate value and calculate the ultimate value simultaneously.
3. This makes more sense intuitively than starting at 'base case = 1' when starting from the last step and working backwards. Instead, we start with 0 paths to reach the 0th step (penultimate) and 1 path to reach the 1st step (ultimate), then build up from there. After n loops, our last (ultimate) step can be returned directly.

CommentText: Writing this as someone who switched to FF14 around 3 years ago and has no plans to return to RS3 ever. RS3 (originally RS2) was my childhood game since I was poor and couldn't afford World of Warcraft. I maxed out in RS3, but I wasn't even close to completionist cape levels. RS3 became unenjoyable for me specifically for the reasons you mentioned: 1. Anything I grinded for in the game was pointless. Waiting for daily rewards, treasure hunter keys, or buying bonds is at least 10 times more efficient than any activity I could do to progress in the game. 2. The minigames are totally dead. I don't want to join a specific Discord server to sign up for events. I want to play Stealing Creations whenever I feel like it. 3. (I'm not sure if you mentioned this) The art styles, overworld quality, and NPC model quality are insanely inconsistent. Just walk around the desert; you'll find areas that look like Minecraft chunk borders, enemy models from 2009, and super fancy new stuff all next to each other. 4. I don't have the patience to start over from scratch to play Ironman. I've already invested thousands of hours into the game and don't have the same motivation to level up my skills as when I was a kid. The fact that I'd have to pay for 2 memberships is just the icing on the cake. These are just the reasons that come to mind, and if I bothered reinstalling the game, I could probably give you more. I'm now enjoying FF14, recently cleared my third Ultimate (UwU, TEA, FRU), and I'm currently watching my younger brother experience the main story. I also got an IRL friend, who I originally introduced to RS3, to join me in FF14. She has also quit RS3 completely since then.

I continued working my main job in medical, but stopped working as a first responder for a little bit after that.

I'm so glad this guy wasn't alone, and his friends, real heroes, were able to save him.

World War III Has Begun; How It Unfolds Depends on Us
We think of the Russia-Ukraine war as a local conflict, but it is much more than that; it is a global war on multiple fronts. The war is not only a military conflict; it is also an economic war of attrition. With skyrocketing gas prices and shortage of staples, people all over the world are feeling the consequences of the war.
This war is transforming the entire modus operandi of humanity. Since the dawn of time, we have been accustomed to living by the motto, â€œsurvival of the fittest.â€ By and large, the rule was that the strong determined the rules, and the rules were often abusive toward the weak. Now, it seems like a new mindset has set in: Wanting something and being strong enough to take it does not mean that the world will accept it.
The war, therefore, is being fought on the inside no less, and perhaps more than on the outside. Our very makeup is changing from abusive to cooperative, from narcissistic to altruistic.
It hurts, and it will not happen without a struggle, but it is irreversible. This is the path of our evolution toward the purpose of our creationâ€”to encompass within us all of creation. To do that, we must come to care for it, just as a mother encompasses her child through her maternal love.
The struggle to transition from our current uncaring and mean approach to all creations but ourselves, into wise and compassionate beings is called â€œthe war of Gog and Magogâ€ or Armageddon.
Since the war is about our inner makeup, we can fight it within us. If we object to struggling with ourselves over who will ruleâ€”the ego or loveâ€”the physical reality will force us to choose love nonetheless. However, it will do so by hurting us in a very physical way.
The war in Eastern Europe is nothing compared to what we might have to endure if we resist the process. The horrific descriptions of our sages and prophets hint at it, and we would not want to live through it.
Alternatively, we can fight this war within us without firing a single bullet. The choice is in our hands. All we need is to continue in the same direction that nature is already leading us: toward connection. VideoTitle: Diameter of a Binary Tree - Leetcode 543 - Python
CommentText:
Alternative mathematical approach: It made a little more sense to me to return 0 for a Null node. In doing so, you don't need the + 2 in the updating of the result. You are essentially accounting for the parent edge in different ways. I found this approach to come a little more naturally to me, so I'm posting in case it helps anyone!

    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        
        def dfs(root): 
            nonlocal diameter
            if root is None: 
                return 0
            left = dfs(root.left)
            right = dfs(root.right)
            
            diameter = max(left + right, diameter)
            
            return max(left, right) + 1
            
                    
        diameter = 0
        dfs(root)
        return diameter

VideoTitle: Why renewables canâ€™t save the planet | Michael Shellenberger | TEDxDanubia
CommentText:
Let me start by saying I am a big proponent of 'next-gen' nuclear generation.  In this video, Mr. Shellenberger makes excellent points about the downsides of wind and solar - concerns I have as well.  But I would take a different tact, rather than seemingly eliminating these sources from our toolbox.  Since 2017, the date of the data slide used in the video, solar panels have become much more efficient, as we would expect with innovations over time.  Mr. Shellenberger also does not explore how the expansion of 'roof top' solar for individual users reduces (or, in some cases, eliminates for the individual) power needed from powerplants without the need for additional transmission lines.  Today's panels lose an estimated 12-1/2% of their capacity (approx. 2-1/2% in the initial year and .5% p/year thereafter) over the 20 year period Mr. Shellenberger mentions.  It's not 100%, that's a given, but a 20% reduction over, say, 30 years seems an acceptable return.  As for dumping used panels in 3rd world countries, the solution is easy - stop doing that!

Concerning wind turbines, there are several ways to make the impact on birds less deadly.  The simplest, according to the American Bird Conservancy, is location - choosing areas that are less traversed by birds and bats.  Another way is to make turbines taller and the blades shorter.... and yet another is design.  While vertical axis wind turbines are not as efficient, they do improve the amount of energy generated per square meter and are better seen by birds.

I would also question the need to be 100% 'green', especially in the short term and particularly looking that goal practicality.  The Earth does have natural absorption and storage of greenhouse gasses.  We need to reduce our emissions of CO2 and use both natural and technological means to capture carbon until we come into balance with our planet's own mechanisms.

VideoTitle: Linked List Cycle - Floyd's Tortoise and Hare - Leetcode 141 - Python
CommentText:
Here is another easy but O(1) memory solution with only one pointer. 
We can take advantage of the fact that: (-10**5 <= Node.val <= 10**5) as given in te description. 
This means we can use the left space of the integer  to mark if a node has been visited (and unmark it in a later loop). You would iterate over every node and add a big value (ex 1000000) and verify at each iteration of the node.val is greater than 10**5. If it is, that mean that we have already marked this node and a cycle exists.

After iterating over the entire list and finding if a cycle exists or not, you can actually reiterate over it to unmark any node (if its value is >10**5).
This is basically O(n) compute and O(1) memory with only one pointer.

VideoTitle: I Played Runescape 3 for 100 hours - should you?
CommentText: I realize this topic has been beaten to death, and that RS has had EOC for longer than it didn't, but frankly it's what ruined the game for me. I didn't feel like starting over from the beginning when they released "OSRS," since I was already almost maxed out at that point. It felt like they pulled the rug out from under the game I loved. Something as fundamental as armor became useless overnight. And every content update since then has only made it worse. It was like they changed the main combat experience to be like the pure pvp experience used to be - except it wasn't optional like pures were. Spending tens of millions on higher-level armor, instead of leaving the slots empty, made as much difference on damage reduction as a pure changing their chaps from green to black dragonhide: you'd still get destroyed by everything. Void Knight armor, with its 10% damage bonus, was actually better than all other armor, because that was the most any armor actually contributed to combat. And I say this after returning to see what RS had become and trying to give it a fair chance. I even got 120 necromancy and its full t95 set, plus near-bis gear and loadouts for all the other styles too. They advertised a "combat rework" update. Spoiler: all they did was "rebalance" the dps of the core 3 styles' t95 weapons to match Necromancy's max t95 suite, which got its damage from a weapon and a full set of t95 'armor', and a skill cap of 120 instead of 99. There wasn't any mention of the 'rework' addressing defense or armor at all, and the 'community' reacted like I was insane for bringing it up. And here's the catch: It might not seem that bad initially. EOC doesn't *seem* that broken at first, at lower levels. It seems to work as intended in Daemonheim. But as soon as you start doing high-level Slayer, or any boss above lvl 70, EVERYTHING hits constantly like your armor doesn't exist. Prayer only blocks half of it, or is actively punished. And that's where the main gameplay is. Value creep of drops and gear upkeep makes all older (weaker) mobs not even worth your time. Jagex 'balanced' high-end combat around the assumption that players use every possible consumable, overhead prayer, and Soul Split 100% of the time. I'm serious. They're so out of touch, they 'balance' all combat from the top down around a single quest asset that requires 92 Prayer, and prayer flicking between that and the protection/deflection overheads. ...Your only real way to mitigate damage is Prayer. Not defense, not armor - you know, the things specifically designed for that purpose. Nope. It's Prayer. And a few miscellaneous trinkets like Auras, and a Shadow spell from Necromancy. Oh, and Magic had a defensive spell for a while. It was really popular because it gave us a taste of what we'd lost - and it was nerfed into oblivion.

VideoTitle: Dodgy Claims, Decent Value? - Our Thoughts on Nvidia RTX 5090, 5080, 5070 Ti, 5070
CommentText: I believe the most concerning aspect of these newly announced GPUs is that I'm hearing many content creators say, "Well, it could have been worse." Do you remember when the release of new GPUs was genuinely exciting? When they offered good price-to-performance ratios? NVIDIA seems to have conditioned us into accepting higher prices while depending on frame generation and upscaling to provide actual performance gains, and it seems to have sadly worked. I honestly don't mind utilizing DLSS that much, but I dislike relying on frame gen in most of the games I play. A majority of the performance enhancements are achieved using their latest version of frame generation. They shifted from comparing 30 series cards against 40 series cards utilizing frame generation, to now comparing 40 series cards against 50 series cards using their newer proprietary frame gen, which is exclusive to those GPUs. The charts for Far Cry 6 and A Plague Tale show that the cards are only approximately 20-25% more potent without frame generation, and it has reached a point where they are almost entirely relying on upscaling and AI to make their products viable, even in the higher-end cards that now cost an exorbitant amount.

CommentText:
I will pick a single fruit from the box which is labelled as "Apples + Oranges". Now we know that every box is labelled wrong so in "Apples + Oranges" labelled box we can't have Apples + Oranges. Suppose we get an apple from "Apples + Oranges" labelled box. So we got to know that "Apples + Oranges" labelled box contains only Apples since it can't contain Apples + Oranges. Then we have two boxes more to guess - one which has only oranges and one which has both apples and oranges. Now the box labelled "Oranges" cannot contain only oranges since all labels are wrong. So it must either contain Apples + Oranges or only Apples. But we already know that the box labelled "Apples + oranges" contains only apples. Since we can't have two boxes that contain only apples, the box labelled "Oranges" must contain Apples + Oranges. Therefore the remaining box i.e. the one labelled as "apples" must contain only oranges.

LABEL                                          ACTUAL
Apples + Oranges                       Apples
Oranges                              Apples + Oranges
Apples                                         Oranges


Similarly if on opening the "Apples + Oranges" labelled box if we get oranges, then the solution would be
LABEL                                        ACTUAL                          
Apples + Oranges                    Oranges
Oranges                                     Apples
Apples                                Apples + Oranges                         

So just by picking a single fruit from  "Apples + Oranges" labelled box, we can solve the puzzle.

CommentText: "most languages" meaning C/C++/C#? A lot of your remarks about "most languages" don't hold true for Lua, Ruby, JavaScript, Perl, PHP, Io, etc. Python's fundamental behavior generally aligns with other dynamically-typed languages (which also tend to be interpreted). Also, instead of saying a variable's type is assigned at runtime and can change, I'd phrase it as "variables are references to values, and **values** possess types. You can think of it like a sticker, where you can reassign the variable to a different value later." This also clarifies why `i++` doesn't work. If you have i=7 and then wrote i++ you don't want change the value 7 to be 8; that would be terrible if integers were mutable. You want to re-assign i to be a label on a new value. (Which isn't to say i++ couldn't be syntax sugar for i = i + 1, but it does help clarify what's happening.)

VideoTitle: Subsets - Backtracking - Leetcode 78
CommentText: I believe the time complexity is O(n^2 + 2^n). Can someone check my reasoning? The number of subsets is 2^n, while the number of nodes in the binary decision tree is actually 2^(n+1) - 1. So traversing all nodes takes O(2^(n+1) - 1), simplifying to O(2^n). At each leaf node, of which there are (n + 1) / 2, a copy of the subset is created. So, this takes (n+1)/2*n = O(n^2). The overall time complexity is then O(n^2 + 2^n), possibly reducible to O(2^n)?

It's not an absurd situation, it's a result of trademark law and the ownership rights Oracle received when it bought out Sun Microsystem's assets.

In the mid-90s - perhaps before you were born - Sun Microsystems staff (James Gosling et al) invented the Java programming language.  As a good corporation, Sun maintained ownership of the trademarks which required defending the trademarks by notifying folks of any misuse.  The big lawsuit between Sun Microsystems and Microsoft was not over trademarks, but some other issues that are outside the scope of this discussion.

In 1995ish, Netscape engineers developed what's now known as JavaScript as part of the Netscape browser.  Naming it JavaScript was because Sun made a deal with Netscape around the development, and insisted that the language have that name, with Sun owning the trademark JavaScript.  The idea was for JavaScript, and Java Applet, code in the browser would be paired against Java Servlets running on the server side, and it would be full stack Java long before the "fullstack" idea was developed.

Oracle owns Java SE, Java EE, etc, plus the JavaScript trademarks, because it bought out Sun's assets in 2009.

I worked at Sun in the Java SE team during a large portion of that time frame.

CommentText: Personally, I found this to be a rather convoluted explanation of the Fibonacci sequence. Here's how I conceptualize it (it's essentially the same, just a different way of thinking, which some might find simpler). Thinking in reverse, what was the last "move" we executed? We either took a single step or two steps. This implies that if f(n) represents the function that calculates the number of steps to reach the n-th step, then f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2). Continuing this line of reasoning, you'll observe that it aligns with your decision tree diagram: f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) = (f(n-2) + f(n-3)) + f(n-2), and so on. We can readily recognize this as the Fibonacci sequence, and we can even illustrate it with examples: To reach the first step (f(1)), there's only one way. For two steps (f(2)), there are two ways (2 or 1+1). Consequently, to reach three steps (f(3)), we simply sum the preceding two: f(3)= f(2)+f(1) = 2+1 = 3, f(4)=f(3)+f(2) = 3+2=5, f(5)=f(4)+f(3)=5+3=8, and so forth. Depending on the desired programmatic solution, we can then select an appropriate approach.

VideoTitle: Getting Started With Chart.js
CommentText: I must disagree, this isn't suitable for beginners. It appears geared towards experienced coders. It's also not very practical, and it's challenging to implement on platforms like Drupal. Usually, chart data is present within the HTML, as site content. Regular users don't have the ability to access CSS or JavaScript; they're limited to an editor for standard HTML, in tables or lists. That's where the chart data usually resides.  The script part is inaccessible, but it needs to gather data from the HTML. While possible, it's not straightforward and certainly not beginner-friendly. A more user-friendly approach would be to use a HTML table with a specific class containing the data, and a class for the chart type. A lot more work is needed to handle every aspect of how a chart is displayed.

I followed both this course and the official material. Stuff covered in the official material and the product cheat sheet they provide is more than enough to prepare this new version of the exam. I don't know if/when they changed the content of the exam again, but none of the questions you find online were present in my test (or even similar). This was my experience. This course was great nevertheless, it really helped cement the concepts and help you really understand the products, so thanks for providing it!

If that tables p_key is not referenced in another table we call it seq if another table does use it, its called id so a user table would have a column id, then on the table referencing there would be a sequence and a column called user_id.

All of out many to many tables we call tablename_xref (xref for cross-reference) so just looking at the database it makes a ton of sense. we also add control columns on every table prefixed with ctl we have an insert user, insert time, update user, update time the times are stored as dttm (time with timezone). any anytime a user inserts data or updates data its reflected in the control columns.
